newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Last-minute hitches delay $610 mln award to Kuwait.
newsitem.headline: Last-minute hitches delay $610 mln award to Kuwait.

text.p: Approval of a $610 million award to the Kuwait Oil Company for the cost of putting out oil well fires set by Iraqi troops was delayed on Monday after Egypt and France raised last-minute issues, U.N. sources said.
But the sources, who asked not to be named, said they expected the claim to be formally approved on Tuesday when the Governing Council of the U.N. Compensation Commission resumes.

France and Egypt, and to a lesser extent Indonesia and Russia, raised largely technical questions about the damages award recommended by a panel of three arbitrators who assesed Kuwait's $950 million claim, according to diplomats.
A Western diplomat said: "It wouldn't surprise me if there are political motivations behind it. But I have no reason to believe it will be delayed based on what I heard today.
"If I had to bet, I'd say it will go through," he added.
A U.N. source said: "I expect a decision tomorrow (Tuesday). It would be a tragedy after four years if the Governing Council does not take a decision which it is obligated to do."
The first corporate claim assessed by the Gulf War reparations body, the well blow-out is of great symbolic importance to the emirate.

At the end of the Gulf War in February 1991, when a coalition of Western and Arab forces led by the United States drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait after a seven-month occupation, nearly 800 oil wells were set alight. Some burned for months.
The neutral judges, named by the Geneva-based fund, have recommended KOC be awarded $610 million of its total $950 million claim for damages, according to diplomats.
They recommended that nearly $340 million be considered under another claim category. A small sum was rejected.
The Governing Council, composed of officials from the 15 Security Council member-states, examined the judges' report, which remains confidential. They extended talks for one day.
Some Western diplomats said Iraq had been trying to block the KOC claim from being decided. In the past, Baghdad has argued that the fires were a result of Allied bombing.
"Iraq is going all over town complaining that the well-blow claim should be put aside or thrown out," a diplomat said.

Abdul Rahman Al-Houty, former chairman of Kuwait's Public Authority, in a December 1994 statement, referred to the KOC claim as "the most notorious and injurious of all the many direct losses" suffered as a result of Iraq's unlawful invasion.
Iraqi deputy foreign minister Riyadh al-Qaysi lobbied the Governing Council last July to set aside money to mount a legal defence against claims, saying the embargo deprived it of funds.

During oral hearings on the case, al-Qaysi also asked that consideration of the well-blow claim be suspended to give Baghdad more time to prepare its case. But the panel rejected the bid, prompting the Iraqi delegation to walk out.

The UNCC, set up by the Security Council to assess claims from individuals, firms, and governments for losses caused by Iraq's invasion and occupation, has received claims totalling $200 billion. But its funding, so far dependent on government donations and seized Iraqi assets, has been precarious.

The fund has been buoyed by recent implementation of the oil-for-food deal between the United Nations and Iraq. Under the six-month renewable deal, the UNCC is to receive 30 per cent of oil export revenues -- meaning about $100 million a month.
UNCC's share of revenues should enable it to begin paying substantial reparations to individual claimants by March.
To date, it has only been able to pay out $13.4 million in awards to 4,000 priority claimants for death of a close relative or serious personal injury.
